title: Resources
definition: An MCP Resource is a URI-addressable, read-only piece of context — a file, record, log, schema, etc. — that a server exposes via `resources/read` for the *host application* (not the model) to decide when to attach to a conversation.
summary: Resources are MCP's data primitive: servers advertise them through `resources/list` (fixed URIs) or `resources/templates/list` (RFC 6570 templates), and clients fetch content through `resources/read`, getting back `text` or base64 `blob` per item. The `resources` capability negotiated at `initialize` declares two independent flags — `subscribe` (per-resource update pushes) and `listChanged` (the available set changed). Unlike Tools, which the model invokes on its own judgment, attaching a Resource to context is an application/user decision — that control-model distinction is exactly what interviewers probe for.
objectives: Explain the control-model split between Resources (application-driven), Tools (model-driven), and Prompts (user-driven).
Implement `resources/list`, `resources/templates/list`, and `resources/read`, handling both `text` and base64 `blob` content.
Describe the `resources` capability's `subscribe` and `listChanged` flags and when each is worth the added server state.
Identify production risks: URI validation/path traversal, unbounded single-resource size, and list-vs-content pagination.
Recognize that a model cannot pull a Resource into context on its own — it only works with what's already attached.
lesson:
MCP gives servers three ways to add value to a session, split by *who decides*: Tools are model-controlled — the LLM invokes them mid-reasoning; Prompts are user-controlled — picked from a menu; Resources are application-controlled — the host or orchestration layer decides what data to attach. Resources model *data*, not *actions*: a file, a DB row, a log tail, a config blob.

Every resource has a `uri`, `name`, optional `description`, and optional `mimeType`. Static ones are advertised via `resources/list`; parameterized ones via `resources/templates/list`, which returns RFC 6570 templates like `file:///{path}` that a client fills in before calling `resources/read`. A read returns one or more content items, each with a `uri`, `mimeType`, and *either* `text` (UTF-8) *or* `blob` (base64) — never both, and binary content always pays roughly a 33% base64 size tax.

Worked intuition: in a code-review assistant, the repo's files are Resources — a file picker lets a user attach `file:///src/auth.py`. Whether to run a linter on it is a Tool call — the model decides that autonomously based on what it sees. That split keeps "what data enters context" auditable and host-controlled, while "what actions happen" stays under model judgment. The most common design mistake is expecting the model to reach out and pull a resource into its own context on its own initiative: without a Tool wrapping the fetch, the model can only work with resources it has already been handed.

Building on capability negotiation: a server that supports resources declares the `resources` capability at `initialize` with two independent flags — `subscribe` (clients may call `resources/subscribe` on a URI and get pushed `notifications/resources/updated`) and `listChanged` (the server may push `notifications/resources/list_changed` when the available set changes, e.g. a new log file rotates in). Skipping both just means the client polls `resources/list`/`resources/read` on a timer — correct, just wasteful at scale.

Gotcha for production: MCP's pagination (`cursor`) applies to *listing* resources, not to the *content* of one large resource — `resources/read` on a 2 GB file returns it whole. Chunking an oversized resource is the server's job, not the protocol's.
tradeoffs: Resources are cheap to expose — read-only, no side effects, easy to cache and list liberally — but they push the "what enters context" decision onto the host/orchestration layer; if that layer is unsophisticated, useful data never reaches the model. Subscriptions buy freshness without polling but cost the server per-subscriber state and fan-out — worth it for a handful of actively-watched resources (a live log, a running job), not "subscribe to everything." Prefer a Resource for anything static/read-only and identifiable by URI; reach for a Tool instead when the model must decide dynamically, mid-turn, what to fetch or with what parameters — a resource template it can't invoke itself is the wrong fit for that.

diagnosticQuiz.q: Which statement best defines an MCP Resource?
choices: A capability flag exchanged during the `initialize` handshake
A reusable prompt template a user selects from a menu
A named function the model can invoke to perform an action or computation
A URI-addressable, read-only piece of context that a host fetches via `resources/read` and injects into the conversation
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: Resources are the "data" primitive — addressable by URI, fetched read-only through `resources/read`, and attached to context by the application/user rather than invoked by the model. Option A describes a Tool and C describes a Prompt; D describes the negotiation mechanism that *advertises* Resources, the classic trap of conflating a primitive with the handshake that announces it.

diagnosticQuiz.q: A server exposes a 300 KB binary file as a Resource. The client reads it and gets a `blob`. Approximately how large is that payload on the wire?
choices: ~900 KB, base64 triples binary size
~400 KB, from base64's ~4/3 expansion
~300 KB, no change
~150 KB, base64 compresses binary
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: Base64 encodes every 3 raw bytes as 4 ASCII characters, roughly a 33% size increase, so 300 KB becomes ~400 KB. "No change" is the tempting wrong answer — the misconception that MCP's JSON-RPC transport is somehow binary-transparent, when anything not sent as `text` pays the encoding tax.

diagnosticQuiz.q: Why can't the model, mid-turn, silently pull in an MCP Resource the way it invokes a Tool?
choices: Resources are always too large for the context window
Attaching context is an application/user-controlled decision by design, not a model-initiated action
The protocol has no `resources/read` method
Resources require a database connection Tools don't
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: MCP's control model deliberately separates *who decides*: Tools are model-controlled, Resources are application-controlled, Prompts are user-controlled — a split that keeps context injection auditable. Treating Resources as "Tools without an invocation step" is the core misconception the other options gesture at.

diagnosticQuiz.q: You're designing an MCP server for a CI system. Which is the better fit for a Resource rather than a Tool?
choices: "Re-run the failing job" — an action with a side effect
"Cancel a running deployment"
"The last 200 lines of job #4521's log" — read-only data referenced by ID
"Search all logs for a regex the model decides on the fly"
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: A log tail addressable by job ID is exactly the static, URI-referenceable data Resources model well — expose it as `logs://{job_id}/tail` and let the host attach it. The other three involve the model deciding, at reasoning time, what action or dynamic query to run — that's Tool territory.

diagnosticQuiz.q: A server holds one 2 GB log file behind a single Resource URI. Which statement about handling it is correct?
choices: `resources/list`'s cursor-based pagination automatically chunks it for you
MCP has no built-in chunking for a single resource's content — the server must enforce size limits or paginate at the application layer itself
The `listChanged` capability splits large resources on updates
`resources/read` always streams content lazily, so size is never a concern
diagnosticQuiz.explanation: List-level pagination (`cursor`) paginates *how many resources are listed*, not the *content of one large resource* — reading it still returns the whole blob/text in one response unless the server designs its own chunking (e.g. separate URIs per range). Conflating list pagination with content pagination is the wrong answer most candidates reach for.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you decide whether a piece of server functionality should be modeled as an MCP Resource or a Tool?
interviewQuestions.a: Ask *who decides when this enters the conversation*. If it's static, read-only data referenced by identity (a file, row, log, schema) that a human or orchestrator chooses to attach, make it a **Resource** — cheap, cacheable, auditable. If the model must decide dynamically, mid-turn, whether to invoke it and with what parameters, make it a **Tool**. Also check for side effects: nothing behind a Resource read should mutate state — if "reading" increments a counter or triggers a job, it belongs behind a Tool instead.

interviewQuestions.q: Your MCP server exposes hundreds of resources (e.g. every file in a large repo). What production concerns come up, and how do you address them?
interviewQuestions.a: Use `resources/templates/list` (e.g. `file:///{path}`) instead of enumerating every file so the set stays derivable rather than a giant literal list; paginate the listing call itself with `cursor`. Validate URIs server-side to block path traversal (`../../etc/passwd`), since the read handler runs with server privileges, and enforce access control per URI rather than trusting the client's requested path. Avoid returning oversized single resources unchunked — cap size or split logically. Once the set is large, prefer `listChanged` notifications over clients polling `resources/list` on a timer.

interviewQuestions.q: Explain the `subscribe` and `listChanged` resource-capability flags and the production tradeoff between them.
interviewQuestions.a: Both are declared under the `resources` capability at `initialize`. `subscribe: true` lets a client call `resources/subscribe` on a specific URI and get pushed `notifications/resources/updated` when that resource's *content* changes — good for a small number of "hot" resources a UI keeps open (a live log tail). `listChanged: true` lets the server push `notifications/resources/list_changed` when the *set* of available resources changes, not any one resource's content. Tradeoff: subscriptions cost per-connection state and fan-out proportional to subscriber count, so they're worth it for a few actively-watched resources, not "subscribe to everything" — at scale, coarser polling or re-reading on demand after a `list_changed` push is cheaper and simpler.
